question: When a disease is constantly present in a specific community or region, what is it called?

options.A: A sudden spike of cases across the globe
options.B: A disease regularly found in a specific area
options.C: A rare illness with no known cure
options.D: An infection that only affects newborn babies

explanation: Great job! An endemic disease is one that stays around in a particular area at a steady, predictable level. Think of it as a familiar visitor in that region. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T15#GNS313_U1_T15_h1)

question: When does a health situation officially become an epidemic?

options.A: When case numbers suddenly rise above the normal expected baseline
options.B: When the causative organism is a drug-resistant bacteria
options.C: When it spreads to at least three different continents
options.D: When hospitals run out of basic treatment medications

explanation: You've got this! An epidemic happens when there is an unusual surge of cases in a community—basically, way more people falling sick than what healthcare workers normally expect to see. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T15#GNS313_U1_T15_h1)

question: In the epidemiological triangle, what does the 'host' refer to?

options.A: The human or animal that carries the infectious organism
options.B: The specific microorganism causing the sickness
options.C: The medication used to treat the infection
options.D: The physical climate where the outbreak takes place

explanation: Spot on! The host is simply the living creature—like you, me, or an animal—that provides a home for the disease-causing germ. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T15#GNS313_U1_T15_h2)

question: Poor drainage and overcrowding in a neighborhood are examples of which part of the epidemiological triangle?
explanation: Well done! Surroundings, living conditions, and sanitation factors make up the 'environment' part of the triangle, which greatly influences how diseases spread. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T15#GNS313_U1_T15_h2)

question: What is meant by a disease 'reservoir'?

options.A: Where the infectious agent normally lives and multiplies
options.B: The Department of Health data storage unit
options.C: A device used to measure patient body temperature
options.D: The specific medication given to kill a virus

explanation: Correct! A reservoir is the natural hiding and breeding place—whether in humans, animals, or soil—where a germ thrives and reproduces. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T15#GNS313_U1_T15_h3)

question: A nurse tells a patient with diarrhea to wash their hands well after using the toilet. Which part of the chain of infection is this stopping?
explanation: You're doing great! Handwashing washes germs away, stopping them from traveling to new surfaces or other people through contact. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T15#GNS313_U1_T15_h3)

question: Which animal serves as the natural home or reservoir for the Lassa virus?
explanation: Exactly! The multimammate rat carries the Lassa virus and sheds it in its urine and droppings, which can accidentally contaminate our food. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T15#GNS313_U1_T15_h4)

question: During the dry season in northern Nigeria, a patient presents with a very stiff neck, high fever, and confusion. What should you suspect first?
explanation: Spot on! A stiff neck and high fever are classic warning signs of meningitis, which tends to cause seasonal outbreaks in northern Nigeria during the dry season. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T15#GNS313_U1_T15_h4)

question: Why do public health teams create a clear 'case definition' during an outbreak?

options.A: To determine which pharmaceutical company supplies drugs
options.B: To decide clearly who is counted as having the outbreak disease
options.C: To write a legal penalty for people who refuse treatment
options.D: To calculate the total financial cost of hospital supplies

explanation: You got it! A case definition gives healthcare workers clear, shared rules to correctly identify and count true cases during an outbreak. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T15#GNS313_U1_T15_h5)

question: Why do health workers draw an epidemic curve on a graph during an outbreak?

options.A: To show the timeline of when cases occurred and track the outbreak's progress
options.B: To prove to international donors that funding was spent wisely
options.C: To measure the physical distance between houses in the village
options.D: To predict exactly what the weather will be like next week

explanation: Brilliant! An epidemic curve turns dates into a picture, helping investigators see when infections started and whether the outbreak is slowing down or growing. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T15#GNS313_U1_T15_h5)

question: In Nigerian public health, what does the acronym IDSR stand for?
explanation: Correct! IDSR is the helpful framework our health facilities use to track, report, and respond to important diseases efficiently. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T15#GNS313_U1_T15_h6)

question: Why is active community surveillance just as important as checking hospital record books?

options.A: Community members are better at performing laboratory blood tests
options.B: Government funding requires village meetings every single month
options.C: Many sick people in rural areas never visit a formal health facility
options.D: Hospitals are not allowed to report infectious diseases directly

explanation: You're right on track! Many villagers stay home or go to local chemists when sick, so community-level reporting helps us catch hidden cases that hospitals might miss. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T15#GNS313_U1_T15_h6)

question: What is the main difference between isolation and quarantine?

options.A: Isolation separates sick people, while quarantine restricts exposed healthy people
options.B: Quarantine takes place in a hospital, while isolation happens at home
options.C: Isolation is used only for bacteria, while quarantine is used for viruses
options.D: Isolation involves medication, while quarantine involves vaccination only

explanation: Well reasoned! Isolation keeps already-sick people away from others, while quarantine is for healthy people who were exposed and might come down with the illness. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T15#GNS313_U1_T15_h7)

question: As a nurse managing a cholera treatment camp, what is your most critical intervention for saving lives immediately?

options.A: Aggressive rehydration using oral rehydration salts and intravenous fluids
options.B: Strict isolation of patients in a dark, soundproofed room
options.C: Immediate quarantine of all healthy family members in their homes
options.D: Immediate administration of broad-spectrum topical skin ointments

explanation: Spot on! Cholera causes rapid, severe fluid loss, so replacing those fluids quickly with ORS and IV drips is the number one life-saving step. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T15#GNS313_U1_T15_h7)

question: During a disease outbreak, which of these is a core duty for a community health nurse?

options.A: Writing national health policies and approving federal budgets
options.B: Isolating entire towns by deploying armed security forces
options.C: Conducting contact tracing and educating community members on prevention
options.D: Manufacturing vaccines inside local primary health care clinics

explanation: You got it! Nurses are right on the frontline—tracking down contacts, teaching families how to stay safe, and helping at the grassroots level. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T15#GNS313_U1_T15_h8)

question: Which of the following is NOT a reason why nurses must follow strict infection control during an epidemic?

options.A: To prevent the nurse from contracting the infectious agent
options.B: To protect other vulnerable patients admitted to the ward
options.C: To stop the hospital environment from spreading the disease
options.D: To guarantee that patients pay their hospital bills on time

explanation: Brilliant! Infection control is entirely about safety and stopping the spread of germs, and has nothing to do with hospital bills or payments. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T15#GNS313_U1_T15_h8)
